title: What happens in the brain during an orgasm?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore what happens in the brain during an orgasm, starting with dictionary definitions and the body's nerve pathways (pudendal, hypogastric, pelvic, and vagus nerves), including research showing vagus nerve signaling lets paraplegic women reach orgasm. They cover the brain's reward circuit and dopamine, the role of regions like the nucleus accumbens, ventral tegmental area, amygdala, and cerebellum, and hormones such as oxytocin, prolactin, and beta endorphins. They discuss Dutch PET and fMRI studies comparing male and female brains, the deactivation of the orbitofrontal cortex, orgasmia linked to SSRIs, persistent sexual arousal syndrome, non-genital and phantom limb orgasms, a recent fMRI film of a woman's brain during orgasm, and evolutionary theories such as the byproduct theory and twin studies. The episode ends with a contest announcement and a listener mail about gene patenting and the Henrietta Lacks cell line.

entities.name: The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks

segments.title: Opening banter and listener concern about the topic
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with small talk, then Josh recounts receiving the episode suggestion and his worry about covering it. Chuck explains why they will cover sexuality frankly, noting American puritanism versus acceptance of violent topics. They joke about sex education and parental discretion.

segments.title: Definitions of orgasm
segments.summary: The hosts read definitions of orgasm from the Oxford English Dictionary, Merriam-Webster, and Alfred Kinsey, and discuss Shane Freeman's debunking of the sneezing comparison as an urban myth.

segments.title: Where orgasm begins: genital nerve endings
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the nerve density of the clitoris, penis, and glans, including claims about circumcised and uncircumcised penises, which they dismiss as propaganda. They introduce the idea that signals travel from genitals to the brain.

segments.title: Nerve pathways: pudendal, hypogastric, pelvic, and vagus nerves
segments.summary: The hosts describe the hypogastric, pelvic, pudendal, and vagus nerves and what each carries. The vagus nerve bypasses the spinal cord and goes directly to the brain and also controls swallowing.

segments.title: Orgasm in paraplegics and Komisaruk's research
segments.summary: Research by Barry Komisaruk and Beverly Whipple at Rutgers found that women with severed spinal cords could feel cervical stimulation and reach orgasm, with fMRI showing vagus nerve-related brain activity. The hosts note the significance for people with spinal injuries.

segments.title: Reward circuit, dopamine, and key brain regions
segments.summary: The hosts cover the brain's pleasure or reward circuit, the 1950s rat experiments with self-stimulation, and dopamine release. They describe the amygdala, nucleus accumbens, ventral tegmental area, cerebellum, and pituitary gland.

segments.title: Hormones: oxytocin, beta endorphins, and bonding
segments.summary: The pituitary releases beta endorphins for pain relief and oxytocin for trust and bonding. The hosts link these hormones to childbirth, breastfeeding, and post-sex emotions such as crying.

segments.title: Dutch brain imaging studies and orbitofrontal shutdown
segments.summary: Dutch researchers used PET and then fMRI scans on people during orgasm and found few differences between male and female brains in the pleasure circuit, with similar patterns to heroin. The orbitofrontal cortex shut down in both sexes, while women showed decreased amygdala and hippocampus activity and activity in the insular cortex. The hosts note faked orgasms show a different brain pattern.

segments.title: Orgasmia, SSRIs, and persistent sexual arousal syndrome
segments.summary: The hosts discuss orgasmia, the inability to orgasm, linked to SSRI antidepressants that may reduce dopamine. They describe post-SSRI sexual dysfunction and persistent sexual arousal syndrome, and Dr. Komisaruk's research into both, including meditation as a possible calming technique.

segments.title: Non-genital orgasms, phantom limb orgasms, and the homunculus
segments.summary: The hosts discuss orgasms from stimulation of other body parts such as nipples and orgasms from imagery alone. They describe reports of orgasms felt in phantom limbs and the cortical homunculus map as a possible explanation.

segments.title: Live fMRI film of female orgasm
segments.summary: Chuck describes a recent study in which women in an fMRI machine had their brains imaged through orgasm, producing a video showing activity in the genital cortex, limbic system, cerebellum, frontal cortex, hypothalamus, and nucleus accumbens. The participant wore a head mesh and practiced stillness.

segments.title: Evolutionary origin of the female orgasm
segments.summary: The hosts consider why women have orgasms from an evolutionary standpoint, given many women never experience one. They discuss the byproduct theory, comparing it to male nipples, and a twin study finding that same-sex and opposite-sex twins differ in orgasm patterns, which undermines the byproduct idea.

segments.title: Contest announcement
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh promote a contest that ends December 31, entered through the HowStuffWorks Facebook page, with a prize trip to Atlanta and gift cards.

segments.title: Listener mail on gene patenting and Henrietta Lacks
segments.summary: Jim from New Jersey argues that naturally occurring genes should not be patentable, though new constructed genes can be. Chuck cites Rebecca Skloot's book The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks, describing how a medical sample led to research and profits without benefit to her family.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners, give social media and email contact information, and mention the HowStuffWorks website and iPhone app.
